output:
Peter, I appreciate the payroll experience behind your point. You’re right that an informal advance scheme can leave people perpetually short, create recovery problems when someone leaves, and turn HR into a lender. I also agree that a company shouldn’t pretend to be a bank. But I’d be cautious about assuming that closing the window means the need—or the cost—goes away.

We tried almost exactly that approach in 2025. We closed advances after Finance raised the same concerns, gave two months’ notice, and held a financial-literacy session with the SACCO. In the six months that followed, reception logged 61 calls from debt collectors and loan apps. Some were calling supervisors whose names employees had listed as referees. That isn’t a complete measure of what staff borrowed, of course, but it was a concrete sign that at least some of the need had shifted elsewhere.

We also saw more unplanned absence on the two days after month-end. Our fleet manager linked at least three missed Mombasa runs to drivers being away “sorting out” loans. I wouldn’t claim that every absence was caused by closing advances, or that those three runs tell the whole story. But it’s worth comparing the visible costs of a controlled scheme—administration and occasional write-offs—with costs that can be scattered across reception, supervisors, payroll and operations.

The SACCO is a sensible option for planned borrowing, and I agree with encouraging people to use it. But it took two to three weeks to process a loan and required guarantors. That doesn’t help much when a child has been sent home from school over fees on a Tuesday. And financial literacy can help people make better decisions, but it can’t make an urgent bill wait until the next SACCO cycle.

We reopened in September with written rules, rather than returning to the old informal arrangement. Requests go through the payroll portal, not through my office. There’s a maximum of 40% of net pay, once per pay cycle, with the amount repaid in full at the next payroll. There’s no fee. Before approval, we also check the Employment Act’s limit on total deductions: they must not exceed two-thirds of wages. The aim is to ensure that a person isn’t left with nothing at month-end.

Since reopening, we’ve received around 55–70 requests a month, averaging about KES 9,000. We’ve recovered everything except for two employees who left; the total written off for the year is roughly KES 14,000. That’s not an argument that every employer should offer advances, or that our numbers will translate directly to Brenda’s workplace. It is a set of figures she can weigh against the alternatives, rather than treating the choice as cost-free closure versus an unpredictable open tap.

One case that stuck with me was a loader at our Changamwe depot who had taken loans from six apps and was borrowing from one to repay another by the time he came to me. It took payroll and us four months to help unwind that situation. I don’t offer that as proof that advances would prevent every such case. But it did make me think about the limits of saying that app borrowing is solely the employee’s own business when collectors are contacting supervisors and the fallout can affect attendance and work.

The change that persuaded our Finance Manager wasn’t an appeal to sentiment. It was making the exposure predictable. The cap gives Finance a fixed ceiling to forecast against, instead of a series of surprise requests. He now defends the scheme himself. That may be the most useful point for Brenda’s meeting: formal controls can address the very concerns that make Finance want to close the scheme.

If Brenda wants something concrete to take into the room on the 18th, she could propose a time-limited trial with a written policy: a cap as a share of net pay, one request per pay cycle, full repayment at the next payroll, no fee, and a clear approval route through payroll rather than informal supervisor discretion. She could also ask Finance and Operations to track requests, repayment and write-offs alongside unplanned absence, missed shifts or runs, and staff time spent dealing with collection calls. Agreeing in advance how those measures will be reviewed would make the trial easier to assess honestly.

Peter, I think your warning is especially valuable because you’ve seen what can go wrong in payroll. My disagreement is narrower: in our experience, simply closing the window didn’t make the underlying pressure disappear, and some of its consequences became harder to see. For Brenda, the choice may not have to be between informal advances and no advances at all. A capped, transparent policy gives her something testable to put beside Finance’s forecast—and a way to judge the results with numbers, not just a feeling.
